/-!
# Erdős Problem 646

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/646](https://www.erdosproblems.com/646)
- [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number
  theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
- [Er97e] Erdős, Paul, *Some of my favourite unsolved problems*. Math. Japon. (1997), 527-537.
- [Be97] Berend, Daniel, *On the parity of exponents in the factorization of $n!$*.
  J. Number Theory (1997), 13-19.
-/

@[expose] public section

open scoped Nat

namespace Erdos646

/--
Let $p_1,\ldots,p_k$ be distinct primes. Are there infinitely many $n$ such that $n!$ is
divisible by an even power of each of the $p_i$?

The answer is yes, proved by Berend [Be97], who further proved that the sequence of such $n$
has bounded gaps (where the bound depends on the initial set of primes).
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/1d7b3f00780b85ed0462e79a1cd5650ee9055655/src/v4.29.1/ErdosProblems/Erdos646.lean"]
theorem erdos_646 : answer(True) ↔
    ∀ S : Finset ℕ, (∀ p ∈ S, p.Prime) →
      {n : ℕ | ∀ p ∈ S, Even (padicValNat p (n !))}.Infinite := by
  sorry

end Erdos646

reformulations.difference: Berend’s abstract states infinitude for the first k primes and positive integers n. Lean quantifies over arbitrary finite sets of primes and allows n = 0.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Every finite prime set is contained in an initial segment of the primes, so infinitude for initial segments implies infinitude for arbitrary finite prime sets. Conversely, each initial segment is a finite prime set. Removing n = 0 does not change infinitude, and the empty prime set contributes a true instance. In scratch.lean, finiteSetPrimeSegmentIff proves equivalence to the positive-index formulation requiring even valuations at every prime p ≤ N; positiveIndicesIff and finiteSetTupleIff separately verify the index and finite-set conventions.

review.notes: Checked the sole declaration, including answer polarity, simultaneous quantification over primes, exceptional valuation inputs, and smallest cases. Factorials are nonzero and primality excludes bases 0 and 1. Kernel-checked scratch proofs establish the exact-even-power characterization; computations and small proofs confirm nontrivial parity behavior. The linked proof implies the reviewed statement: after three tactic-only adjustments for Lean/Mathlib version differences, both its theorem and an adapter to the finite-set statement compile with only propext, Classical.choice, and Quot.sound. Access limitations: erdosproblems.com returned Cloudflare challenges; [Er97e] and the full text of [Be97] could not be retrieved. The accessible original book passage, Berend’s abstract, and Luca–Stănică’s explicit account suffice to verify the declaration and its bounded-gaps remark.
